titre: Spindletop, 1901: A Salt Dome Launches the Oil Age
accroche: On January 10, 1901, a Texas well blasts oil 50 meters into the air. Underneath: a hidden hill of salt that put crude within drilling reach.
contenu_vulgarise:
On January 10, 1901, near Beaumont, Texas, a well reaches a depth of 347 meters and suddenly starts gushing. The jet, nicknamed the Lucas Gusher, shoots more than 150 feet (about 50 meters) into the air and flows at roughly 100,000 barrels a day, an unheard-of figure for the time. It takes nine days to bring the well under control.

## A hill that is nothing like a hill

Pattillo Higgins was looking for a source of natural gas for his Beaumont brickyard, and thought a nearby rise, Sour Spring Mound, hid oil and gas. The future field would take the name Spindletop, after a hill a little farther east. After the failed attempts of the Gladys City company, Higgins teams up with Captain Anthony F. Lucas, the leading American expert on salt-dome formations. Lucas drills to 575 feet before running out of money, then secures additional funding from John H. Galey, James M. Guffey, and Andrew Mellon of Pittsburgh. The deal leaves Lucas with only an eighth share and Higgins with nothing.

## Why salt attracts oil

Spindletop sits on a layer of Jurassic salt, buried under younger sediments. Salt is ductile: under the uneven load of the layers above it, it rises, and as it pierces the overlying layers it penetrates and bends them, generally upward, on contact with the dome. The salt of a dome is largely impermeable: the strata turned up against it form pockets where oil and gas collect, which is what is called an oil trap. A hill of salt invisible at the surface thus becomes a trap underground. The USGS lists 263 known or suspected onshore salt domes in the Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Alabama portion of the Gulf Coast.

## What Spindletop changed

By late June 1901, thirteen wells are gushing on the same dome; by the end of 1902, more than 500 companies have been formed and 285 wells are in operation. Beaumont's population, 10,000, triples in three months. Before Spindletop, oil was mainly used for lighting and as a lubricant: the quantity discovered suddenly makes it economically feasible to burn it as a fuel for mass consumption, and launches the Texas oil boom. The field produces 17,420,949 barrels in 1902, half that in 1903. Gulf Oil and Texaco, now part of Chevron, were formed to develop production at Spindletop. And the exploration repeats: the field inspires wildcatting along the Gulf Coastal Plain, with salt dome fields such as Sour Lake and Saratoga in 1902, Batson Prairie in 1903, Humble in 1905, and Goose Creek in 1908.

carte.punch: A hidden hill of salt launched the oil age in Texas.
carte.idee: On January 10, 1901, a well drilled on the Spindletop salt dome (Texas) gushes 50 meters high and flows at 100,000 barrels a day. The ductile, largely impermeable salt pierces the sedimentary layers and bends them: pockets where oil and gas collect.

quiz.question: Why does a salt dome form an oil trap?
choix: Salt chemically attracts oil molecules dissolved in the surrounding water
Salt, ductile and barely permeable, bends the layers as it rises and forms oil pockets
Oil forms directly from salt under the pressure of the overlying layers
Salt cools the surrounding rock, which condenses the oil present nearby
quiz.explication: Salt rises slowly under the uneven load of the sediments, penetrates and bends the layers it crosses; largely impermeable, it forms with them pockets where oil and gas collect. None of the other proposals describe any real mechanism.
